stories.title: US trade agency to fund study for Thailand-US subsea cable
stories.summary: THUS cable would be an existing "aging" cable linking the two countries
stories.content:
A new subsea cable system linking Thailand to the US is in the works.

The US Trade and Development Agency this week announced funding for a feasibility study to develop a trusted trans-Pacific submarine cable system that connects Thailand, through neighboring countries, to the United States.

The study will help Thailand’s state-owned telco, National Telecom (NT), assess the viability of the Thailand-US Submarine Cable System (THUS).

The 11,500-mile (18,507km) THUS project is designed to replace Thailand’s aging subsea cable connection to the US. The USTDA said the cable could connect Thailand to the US through up to five other Southeast Asian countries – Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Vietnam – while avoiding the South China Sea and “other routes that carry security risks.”

“This activity will help ensure that the critical infrastructure connecting Thailand to the United States is built using trusted technology, protecting sensitive data from exploitation while advancing Thailand’s ambitions to become a regional digital hub,” said Thomas R. Hardy, USTDA’s deputy director. “By supporting the deployment of secure subsea cable systems, we are helping safeguard networks while opening new opportunities for U.S. companies to compete in one of the world’s fastest-growing digital markets.”

NT has selected Florida-based APTelecom LLC to conduct the study. Full details of potential landing points and routes haven’t been shared.

“THUS is a strategic investment in Thailand’s digital future. A modern, trusted, open-access submarine cable system connecting Thailand directly with the United States will strengthen the resilience and diversity of our international networks, support the growth of Thailand’s data center, cloud, and AI sectors, and expand affordable connectivity for a regional market of more than 600 million people,” said Colonel Sanpachai Huvanandana, president of National Telecom Public Company Limited. “USTDA’s support comes at a pivotal moment. By funding the upfront feasibility work, this grant accelerates THUS toward bankability and opens the door to collaboration with leading American technology providers, whose innovation and engineering expertise we look forward to bringing into the project.”

The Asia-America Gateway (AAG) system, led by a consortium including AT&T, NT, Globe, and others, dates back to 2009. It is the only subsea system linking Thailand to the US.

stories.title: TSMC Co-COO Says AI Is Like a 'Three-Year-Old Superman'
stories.summary: A senior Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) executive likened artificial intelligence (AI) to a toddler with extraordinary powers that doesn’t know right from wrong, explaining why the company adopts a cautious approach to using the technology.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Sept 15): A senior Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) executive likened artificial intelligence (AI) to a toddler with extraordinary powers that doesn’t know right from wrong, explaining why the company adopts a cautious approach to using the technology.

The chipmaker to Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc is particularly careful with using AI to handle sensitive research and development information, co-chief operating officer YJ Mii said on Tuesday. He highlighted the risk of leaks or loss of data if employees don’t use AI properly, pointing to incidents in which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC models infiltrated external organisations.

“AI is like a three-year old superman. It can be quite powerful, but it doesn’t know what kind of damage it can inflict,” Mii told students at National Taiwan University, his alma mater. “And it doesn’t know right from wrong,” he said, without elaborating.

The co-COO was responding to a question about the use of AI at work during a career forum with students in Taipei. His comments followed recent episodes in which rogue AI agents infiltrated Hugging Face and other data systems, prompting calls by Dario Amodei and other industry leaders to slow the pace of AI development while they erect safeguards.

TSMC — one of the biggest beneficiaries of the global AI data centre boom — regards the protection of its proprietary technology as paramount.

Mii didn’t comment at length about the debate over the broader dangers of AI to humanity, a discussion now raging from Washington to Beijing. Instead, he focused more on the technology’s impracticality for applications such as cutting-edge chip design.

The executive said the Taiwanese chipmaker doesn’t find AI that useful for now in helping fashion the next-generation of semiconductor technology. TSMC is developing its next-generation A14- and A10-node fabrication technologies, which are constrained by factors such as a lack of capable equipment. AI can’t help with that, Mii said.

stories.title: YTL Power Secures Four More Siemens Gas Turbines to Meet Rising Regional Energy and AI Demand
stories.summary: YTL Power International has secured four additional gas turbines from Siemens Energy through reservation agreements, adding to three units previously reserved for a total of seven. The turbines are intended to serve rising energy demand in the region, including from AI data centers.
stories.why_it_matters: Locking in turbine supply ahead of competitors gives YTL a critical advantage as gas generation equipment faces multi-year global backlogs driven by data center demand. For Malaysia's data center ambitions, domestic control over dispatchable power capacity helps answer the energy security concerns now shaping project approvals.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 15): YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR) said it has acquired four additional gas turbine units from Siemens Energy via reservation agreements.

The new reservations add to the three units previously secured by YTL Power, bringing the total to seven units, with a combined capacity of over 5,250MW, to support power generation projects in Malaysia and the wider region, according to a statement on Tuesday.

The deal supports YTL Power’s efforts to meet growing regional energy needs, driven by industrial growth, electrification, and the rapid expansion of data centres and AI. It also strengthens YTL Power’s existing investments in digital infrastructure, including data centres, YTL AI Cloud and AI models developed by YTL AI Labs.

“Energy is the foundation of the AI economy. By combining our power generation experience with our expanding capabilities in data centres and AI, we are building the infrastructure that will support our customers' growth and the industries of the future,” said YTL Power managing director Datuk Seri Yeoh Seok Hong in the statement.

Siemens Energy’s SGT-9000HL gas turbines are designed to offer high efficiency, operational flexibility and reliable power generation as electricity systems integrate higher levels of renewable energy.

“As demand for data centres accelerates, reliable and resilient power infrastructure will be critical to enabling this growth while strengthening the country's energy security,” Siemens Energy AG and executive vice-president, gas services Karim Amin said.

Shares of YTL Power closed lower at 2.99 or RM5.51 on Tuesday, giving the group a market capitalisation of RM48.11 billion

stories.title: Malaysia's AI Governance Bill to be tabled in Parliament by Q1 2027
stories.summary: Malaysia’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Bill could be tabled in Parliament in Q3 2026 or Q1 2027 as the government moves to implement a framework for regulating the rapidly developing technology. The draft legislation had been completed after the Digital Ministry held workshops and consultations with stakeholders and is now being prepared for submission to […]
stories.content:
Malaysia’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Bill could be tabled in Parliament in Q3 2026 or Q1 2027 as the government moves to implement a framework for regulating the rapidly developing technology. The draft legislation had been completed after the Digital Ministry held workshops and consultations with stakeholders and is now being prepared for submission to the Cabinet.

“The draft has already been completed. Hopefully, it will be tabled in Parliament this quarter or, if not, in the first quarter of next year. For some of these matters, we look first at standards, then regulations and subsequently laws. The ability to formulate regulations is also important, given that AI technology is developing rapidly and new issues may arise at any time,”Gobind Singh Deo, Digital Minister of Malaysia reportedly said recently, as reported by The Star.

Gobind added, “Efforts to establish the enforcement structure are now being pursued concurrently with the process of bringing the Bill to the Cabinet. This integrated approach is important to ensure that governance and enforcement mechanisms are in place when the Bill is passed. The goal is to ensure technology is not just accessible, but actively adopted to deliver real economic benefits.”

The Malaysian government is taking a broader approach to AI governance that includes standards, regulations and legislation, with different issues to be addressed through the appropriate mechanism. The Digital Ministry is working with Sirim Berhad on MY-AI Standards, while some issues could be dealt with through regulations without the need for new laws.

The government is also advancing efforts to establish an effective enforcement mechanism through the formation of AI Malaysia, which is expected to play a key role in overseeing compliance with applicable laws and facilitating enforcement action in cases of non-compliance.

The move towards a comprehensive AI governance framework comes amid the rapid development and adoption of AI technologies, which continue to present emerging legal and regulatory challenges. As these developments outpace existing legislative frameworks, regulators may need to respond to new risks and issues through targeted regulatory measures before they could be formally addressed through legislation.

stories.title: Copyright Proposal Lets AI Giants Train for Free If Quotas Are Met
stories.summary: A Labor government copyright reform proposal shows artificial intelligence giants would be permitted to train their models on all online content without paying its creators if they struck deals with…
stories.content:
A Labor government copyright reform proposal shows artificial intelligence giants would be permitted to train their models on all online content without paying its creators if they struck deals with enough rights holders, even as the government insisted it would not back down on its pledge to protect creative industries.

Documents seen by *The Australian* *Financial Review* reveal copyright proposals under consideration by Attorney-General Michelle Rowland that would allow AI companies to train on “unprotected material online” provided they secure licensing deals with a minimum number of companies, effectively putting the onus on rights holders to “opt out”.

stories.title: Love It or Hate It, Fund Managers Can't Ignore the Firmus Juggernaut
stories.summary: Firmus, the Nvidia-backed AI data center company, has become impossible for Australian fund managers to overlook as its valuation and market presence grow rapidly. The company's rise is forcing institutional investors to take positions on AI infrastructure whether they believe in the thesis or not.
stories.why_it_matters: Firmus's gravitational pull on portfolios shows how AI infrastructure exposure has become a benchmark risk for Australian institutional investors rather than an optional bet. The dynamic channels more capital into data center development but also concentrates risk if AI spending expectations are revised downward.
stories.content:
The penny is starting to drop in investor land about just how big artificial intelligence factory builder Firmus could be – and it’s making the proposed IPO and sharemarket listing even juicier.

Firmus co-chief executive Oliver Curtis and his investor relations boss Toby Langley were hosting offshore investors at JPMorgan in Hong Kong on Tuesday and at Morgan Stanley’s Singapore office on Monday. There’s no information released to Melbourne and Sydney’s fund managers yet, but the market’s fishbowl is small enough that headline numbers have started falling off the back of the Firmus truck.

stories.title: Data centers make up 44pc of total investment into Malaysia in 1H2026
stories.summary: Malaysia's Data Centre Task Force has assessed more than 40 proposals this year from companies seeking to build or expand data centers, weighing investment value against energy, water and connectivity requirements. Data center projects accounted for 44 percent of total investment into the country in the first half of 2026.
stories.why_it_matters: The figures confirm data centers have become Malaysia's single largest investment category, which strengthens the case for tighter government screening of projects based on resource consumption. Operators and investors face a more selective approval environment, while utilities and landholders in established hubs such as Johor stand to gain from continued demand.
stories.content:
Malaysia has received more than 40 proposals this year from companies looking to establish or expand data center operations, even as the government seeks to manage the sector’s growing demands for energy, water and connectivity. Malaysia’s Data Centre Task Force (DCTF) assessed the proposals based on factors including investment value, energy and water consumption, connectivity requirements, and their potential contribution to the country’s long-term economic and digital development, Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister reportedly said during a speech at a recent event in Kuala Lumpur.

“As the scale and pace of investment increase, our priorities must evolve alongside the industry. The next phase is about what that capacity delivers: artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, home-grown innovation, skilled talent and higher-value jobs,” he added.

His speech was delivered on his behalf by Deputy Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Sim Tze Tzin.

The government has strengthened the role of the DCTF, which is co-chaired by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) and the Ministry of Digital, to improve coordination in the data center industry and set standards for power, water and carbon use efficiency as reported by The Edge Malaysia.

“Through the task force, the Energy Commission and the National Water Services Commission are also developing the relevant frameworks and guidelines to support the sustainable development of the data center industry. As the industry continues to grow, we want to see new capacity supported by operators that are committed to renewable energy, greater efficiency and responsible resource management, while adopting more sustainable solutions across their operations,” Johari further said.

Data center and cloud computing projects accounted for RM 95.8 billion (US$ 23.5 billion), or nearly 44 percent of all approved investments in 1H 2026 while data center related investment approvals have reached RM 385.7 billion (US$ 94.7 billion) since 2021, the minister revealed.

Malaysia approved RM 218.5 billion (US$ 53.6 billion) in investments across various economic sectors in the first half of 2026, an increase of almost 12 percent from the same period last year.

stories.title: West River Eyes Higher Margins via Data Centre and High-Voltage Projects
stories.summary: Malaysian mechanical and electrical contractor West River Bhd is shifting its focus toward data center and high-voltage power projects, aiming to capture higher margins from the country's power infrastructure boom. The group is targeting specialized work where technical capability and track record command premium pricing.
stories.why_it_matters: West River's pivot illustrates how Malaysia's data center surge is reshaping the local construction supply chain, pulling contractors up the value chain into specialist roles. As more M&E firms chase the same higher-margin work, competition for skilled labor and qualified contractors could become a bottleneck for project delivery.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 7, 2026 - September 13, 2026

MECHANICAL and electrical (M&E) player West River Bhd (KL:WESTRVR) is leveraging Malaysia’s power infrastructure boom to move up the value chain, shifting its focus towards specialised projects where technical capabilities and execution track record command higher margins.

The group, which provides end-to-end electrical engineering and air conditioning and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) solutions, is increasingly targeting data centres, high-voltage electrical work and high-tech industrial projects.

Managing director Stanley Lim Yong Lai says the strategy is aimed at improving the quality of West River’s order book rather than simply pursuing project volume.

“Basically, we are shifting to more high-margin work,” Lim says in an interview.

Opportunities are particularly apparent in data centres, where West River estimates net margins can reach 12%, compared with about 5%-6% for its traditional projects.

Lim says the difference reflects the more specialised nature of data centre M&E work and the smaller pool of contractors with the technical capabilities and experience required.

“Data centre projects are different. The requirements are higher and there are fewer players,” he says.

West River has secured two data centre projects so far this year worth a combined RM47.76 million, accounting for about 20% of its outstanding order book of RM200 million.

The group also has a tender book of about RM600 million. Lim puts its historical average success rate at about 8%.

Larger projects, however, come with higher performance bond requirements. Lim says West River typically needs to provide a performance bond equivalent to about 10% of the contract value, making funding capacity an important consideration as the group scales up its order book.

As at end-March, West River had RM4.68 million in cash and RM22.33 million in money market funds, against total borrowings of RM5.01 million, leaving it with net cash of about RM22 million.

Lim believes the current data-centre boom cycle may last another two to three years.

The company is, however, not looking to become overly dependent on data centre projects. Instead, it is using the current boom to build capabilities in other areas of the power and M&E ecosystem.

One of the more significant developments at West River is certification from Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) for high-voltage work, which allows it to pursue substation-related projects.

Lim says the group is looking to participate in 132kV and 275kV work, which he believes offers attractive opportunities given the higher barriers to entry.

Contractors need to meet requirements, including Tenaga qualification, ISO standards, and competency tests for engineers and safety personnel before they can participate in the segment.

The qualification could prove particularly timely as Malaysia expands its power infrastructure to support data centres, renewable energy and industrial activity. The rollout of renewable energy projects will also require substations and other grid infrastructure to connect new generation capacity to the electricity network.

For West River, this creates a potential second leg of growth alongside data centre M&E work.

Lim expects the group’s overall net profit margin to progressively improve over the coming years, compared with around 5% to 6% currently, as higher-margin projects account for a greater share of its business.

Another margin-accretive initiative is the group’s move to manufacture its own electrical panels and distribution boards.

The manufacturing operation currently supplies only to West River’s own engineering projects. The group also plans to expand production as its project portfolio grows.

The move is intended not only to improve gross margins but also to give the company greater control over procurement and project execution.

Lim estimates that its in-house manufacturing capability could improve gross margins by about two to three percentage points from the current level of around 12%.

“The first is margin, and the second is that we can control [the supply],” he says.

Greater control over equipment supply could become increasingly important as West River takes on larger and more technically demanding projects, where delivery schedules are critical.

Raw material costs remain a potential headwind, with copper prices being a key factor for the group. Lim says the sharp movement in material prices had affected margins, but the impact has become more manageable.

West River’s changing project mix is also reflected in its business exposure.

Residential projects currently account for about 44% of its business, while commercial and industrial projects account for about 19% and 36%, respectively.

The group is gradually moving away from conventional residential work and directing resources towards commercial and industrial jobs with higher technical requirements such as hospitals, semiconductor facilities and other high-tech industrial projects.

The semiconductor market remains a relatively new area for West River, with Lim describing its current projects as a step towards gaining a foothold in the sector.

“We are still not a main player,” he says. “But we are penetrating in, and there are a lot of opportunities.”

West River is also becoming more selective in the projects it bids for as it seeks to improve the profitability of its order book. While the group continues to pursue projects from existing customers where returns are attractive, it is prioritising new projects that offer better margins and align with its technical capabilities.

The approach underlines the group’s focus on improving the quality of its order book rather than simply growing its size.

Another differentiator for West River is its proprietary Internet of Things system, which focuses on energy management, particularly for air conditioning systems. As air conditioning is one of the largest energy consumers in many commercial buildings, the technology has the potential to help customers reduce electricity consumption.

Lim says the system serves as a value-added offering alongside West River’s M&E services, allowing the group to provide customers with more than just installation work.

The business is still at an early stage, however, and the immediate focus is on deploying the technology and building customer adoption rather than generating recurring fees.

Beyond its core M&E business, West River is developing two mini-hydropower projects with a capacity of about 7.2MW and 4.5MW.

The group has secured Feed-in Tariff (FiT) approval under the Sustainable Energy Development Authority Malaysia (SEDA) framework, with the projects eligible for 21-year power purchase arrangements at tariffs of nearly 34 sen per kWh from August 2031.

The projects could eventually provide West River with a recurring earnings stream while allowing it to capture a portion of the M&E work involved in their development.

Lim estimates M&E could account for up to 40% of the cost of a mini-hydropower project.

The shift in strategy comes after a difficult financial year ended Dec 31, 2025 (FY2025) for West River, during which weaker project activity and margin compression weighed on its earnings and share price.

The company, which debuted on Bursa Malaysia in April 2025 at 39 sen per share, saw its share price hit a low of 19 sen following the announcement of the weaker financial results.

Revenue fell 9.4% to RM111.2 million in FY2025 from RM122.7 million a year earlier, as several major M&E projects moved into the final stages of installation, testing and commissioning.

Gross profit declined 25.9% to RM13.9 million, with gross margin narrowing to 12.6% from 15.3%, amid higher material and subcontractor costs, and a less favourable project mix.

Net profit fell 47.1% to RM6.1 million, while net profit margin shrank to 5.5% from 9.3%. The decline was also partly due to RM600,000 in non-recurring initial public offering (IPO)-related expenses.

The weaker FY2025 performance stands in contrast to West River’s strong growth between FY2021 and FY2024. Revenue more than doubled from RM55.3 million in FY2021 to RM122.7 million in FY2024, while net profit rose from RM3.7 million to RM11.5 million. Net profit margin improved steadily from 6.6% to 9.3% over the same period.

The earnings decline subsequently weighed on investor sentiment, but the company appears to be turning a corner.

For 1HFY2026, West River reported a 56% increase in revenue to RM79.07 million from RM50.67 million a year earlier, while net profit jumped 81.6% to RM4.63 million from RM2.55 million.

Its shares have also staged a sharp recovery, rising nearly 80% over the past month from around 22 sen to 39 sen, its IPO price. The shares closed at 34.5 sen last Thursday, valuing the company at RM123.4 million.

In a non-rated report published on July 23, RHB Investment Bank pegged West River’s fair value at 45 sen, based on a forward price-earnings ratio of 13 times.

The brokerage estimates that the company could generate RM12.3 million in net profit on RM160 million revenue in FY2027, implying a net profit margin of 7.7%.

With a workforce of about 90 people, West River believes it can accommodate a 30% to 40% increase in revenue with its existing resources, providing room to scale without a corresponding increase in overheads.

Its current earnings visibility stands at around two to three years, but Lim acknowledges that the data centre boom will eventually moderate.

For now, the group is focused on making the most of the current investment cycle while maintaining the financial flexibility to pursue opportunities beyond it.

It is also keeping an eye on capital returns. While capital is likely to remain focused on growth for now, Lim says West River could consider dividends once its cash reserves reach about 25% of revenue.

Lim remains West River’s largest shareholder, with a 63.97% stake comprising a 21% direct equity interest and 42.97% held through investment vehicle Neutron Capital Sdn Bhd.

stories.title: Philippines Unveils US$34.4 Billion AI Infrastructure Masterplan
stories.summary: The Philippine government has released the final version of the US$34.4 billion AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan covering 2026 to 2033, aiming to establish the country as a regional AI infrastructure hub. The plan targets a 30-fold increase in AI data center capacity by 2033.
stories.why_it_matters: The masterplan puts state backing behind the Philippines' bid to compete with Malaysia and Indonesia for hyperscale investment, giving investors a policy framework and timeline they previously lacked. Execution risk remains high given the country's power costs and connectivity gaps, but the target alone reshapes how developers rank Southeast Asian markets.
stories.content:
The Philippine government recently unveiled the final version of the US$ 34.4 billion Philippines AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan (PAIIM) 2026-2033 which seeks to position the country as a regional hub for artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to the Philippines News Agency.

Under the plan, the government targets a 30-fold increase in AI data center capacity by 2033, from a baseline of 50MW to 1.5 GW. The first phase is expected to deploy about 400 MW by 2030. The planned AI industry is expected to power about 152,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), a figure being used as a proxy to estimate computing capacity and electricity demand.

The Philippines has an established policy framework for AI, ranking second among ASEAN countries in an AI benchmark, behind Thailand and on par with Singapore, said Gemma Baysic, National ICT Planning, Policy and Standards Bureau Officer-in-Charge Director, Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT). “The Philippines aims to build, host, power, and support the AI ecosystem of the future,” said Baysic.

Immediate power requirements are expected to be met partly through natural gas plants, while the government is targeting renewable sources, including solar and geothermal, to provide 40 percent of the power used by AI infrastructure by 2033. The Department of Energy (DOE) will also examine nuclear power as a longer-term option under Republic Act 12305, or the Philippine National Nuclear Energy Safety Act (PhilAtom Act).

The masterplan identifies six areas to support AI infrastructure development namely connectivity infrastructure, AI compute and data centers, sustainable energy and water sourcing, AI workforce development, policy and regulation, and demand creation and adoption.

It also identifies four corridors where the AI infrastructure will be built. The Clark-Bataan corridor is designated as the primary anchor, while the Batangas-Aurora corridor will serve as a strategic gateway. Subic and Calabarzon are identified as supporting hubs, with Cebu, Iloilo, Davao and Cagayan de Oro designated as future regional nodes.

The US$ 34.4 billion projected investment is expected to come from both public and private sources. US$ 13.5 billion (39 percent) is expected to be financed by public sources, while US$ 21 billion (61 percent) is expected to come from private investors.

The AI-driven productivity gains and new digital services are estimated to increase national GDP by 10 to 12 percent.

The masterplan cites the Philippines’ geographic location, 21 submarine cables, more than 95 percent mobile coverage and 1.3 million-strong IT-BPM workforce as factors supporting its positioning as an AI infrastructure market.

The country currently has only one AI-oriented data center facility with an installed capacity of about 50 MW, highlighting the scale of expansion required to meet projected demand.

stories.title: Google Cloud opens Singapore engineering centre for AI
stories.summary: The site will link AI research with product development, as Google Cloud uses Singapore to build tools for global customers and regional deployment.
stories.content:
Tue, 15th Sep 2026 (Yesterday)
Google Cloud has opened a Singapore Engineering Centre, its first Google Cloud engineering centre in Southeast Asia.

The centre is co-located with Southeast Asia's first Google DeepMind research lab, linking cloud product development and AI research at a single Singapore site.

Google Cloud said the Singapore Engineering Centre will serve as its main product development hub in the region, bringing together software engineers working across AI, AI infrastructure, data, compute, machine learning, networking, storage and frontline support.

The operation is intended to build cloud and AI products in Singapore for global markets. Work includes developing data systems and infrastructure for low-latency and critical business workloads, integrating foundation models into broader cloud products, and building developer platforms and automation tools for hybrid and multicloud environments.

The move expands Google's investment in Singapore's technology sector, after the company outlined plans for the centre earlier this year. The project is backed by the Singapore Economic Development Board, which said it would deepen local expertise in AI and cloud engineering.

“Singapore is proud to host Google Cloud's first Engineering Centre in Southeast Asia. It will add depth and expertise to Singapore's diverse AI and cloud ecosystems by accelerating AI application development and shaping products for global deployment. We welcome Google's continued investment in the Singapore workforce with new core engineering and FDE roles presenting exciting opportunities for Singaporeans to build expertise with frontier technologies,” said Beng Kong Pee, Executive Vice President, EDB.

### Regional role

Google Cloud said the centre marks a shift from the regional operations that often focus on support or post-sales work. Instead, engineers in Singapore will work directly with corporate customers to adapt core Google Cloud systems to business requirements during development.

The company described this as a closer link between research, engineering and customer deployment. By housing AI researchers and cloud systems teams in the same environment, it aims to shorten the path from model research to production software.

Early work at the site includes collaboration with Grab on real-time multilingual AI models and with DBS on financial workflows using AI agents. Google Cloud said those projects are helping shape products that can later be used more widely across its global customer base.

DBS framed the development as part of a broader effort to strengthen Singapore's position in AI. The bank said it expects to work with industry partners as it develops its own use of agentic AI.

“Singapore has the opportunity to be a trusted global AI hub, bringing together talent, technology and enterprise expertise to drive innovation and growth. The opening of Google Cloud's Singapore Engineering Centre is a welcome addition to this ecosystem. As DBS advances our agentic AI strategy, we look forward to collaborating across the industry to deliver value for our employees and customers in a safe and responsible manner,” said Nimish Panchmatia, Chief Transformation and Data Officer, DBS.

### Customer deployment

Alongside the engineering centre, Google Cloud is expanding its regional Forward Deployed Engineer workforce. These teams work with customers to integrate systems built on Google products and help move projects from trial phases into live operations.

Engineers in these roles will build on tools and systems developed at the Singapore hub, giving the operation a dual function: core product engineering and customer implementation through regional technical teams.

For Singapore, the investment also has a workforce dimension. Google and the EDB pointed to new engineering and Forward Deployed Engineer roles as part of the expansion, linking the project to national efforts to build deeper local expertise in AI and cloud technologies.

The announcement comes as large technology companies continue to use Singapore as a base for regional engineering, data and AI work. Its concentration of multinational firms, financial institutions and digital platforms has made it a key market for testing software in sectors such as banking, transport and consumer services.

Google Cloud said that diversity was one reason for choosing Singapore. It said designing systems for Asia Pacific markets, where languages, regulation and customer demands vary widely, can help improve products for broader international use.

“A true test of engineering capability is building for the diversity and speed of Asia Pacific, which is why we chose Singapore. By anchoring the entire AI value chain in Singapore-from foundational research to core Google Cloud SEC productization and hands-on problem-solving and implementation via our Customer Engineering and Forward Deployed Engineer teams-we transform frontier capabilities, in close collaboration with our customers, into ready-to-deploy products at unprecedented speed,” said Moe Abdula, Vice President, Customer Engineering, Asia Pacific, Google Cloud.

stories.title: Micron Taiwan union presses profit-sharing demand, keeps strike preparations alive
stories.summary: Micron's Taiwan union is pressing for a profit-sharing agreement and is keeping strike preparations in place as negotiations continue. Any labour disruption could intensify supply constraints in an already tight memory chip market.
stories.why_it_matters: A strike at Micron's Taiwan operations would tighten DRAM and HBM supply precisely when AI data center buildouts are consuming record volumes of memory. Operators and server buyers could face higher component costs and longer lead times, feeding through to project budgets across the region.
stories.content:
Labour action could amplify supply concerns in an already tight memory chip market

[TAIPEI] A Taiwanese union representing workers at Micron Technology warned on Tuesday (Sep 15) it could move towards a strike unless the US memory chipmaker agrees to a permanent profit-sharing system, escalating a labour dispute at its largest manufacturing hub.

Taiwan is a crucial production centre for Micron’s DRAM and high-bandwidth memory chips, key components in artificial intelligence servers.

While no strike has been called and there has been no impact on production, any labour action could amplify supply concerns in an already tight memory chip market.

The dispute underscores growing pressure on memory chipmakers to share the windfall from the AI boom.

Micron’s Taiwan unions have pointed to South Korean rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which have profit-sharing schemes for employees, in pressing their demands.

The union said it was seeking a long-term, transparent and verifiable profit-sharing system rather than one-off rewards, reiterating its demand that 15 per cent of Micron’s operating profit be allocated to employees globally.

“If there is no concrete proposal on Sep 18 and 21 and employees feel the company is simply dragging out the process, we will declare the negotiations have broken down and move towards a strike vote,” said Jerry Lin, chairman of a union representing workers at Micron’s operations in the northwestern city of Taoyuan.

Micron last week announced fiscal 2026 rewards for more than 60,000 employees globally following what it described as an “extraordinary year” for the company.

Under the scheme, employees in Taiwan who joined before Aug 29, 2025 will receive a T$1 million (US$31,498) cash bonus, while those who joined later will receive a prorated amount.

The union said the new rewards did not address its demand for a permanent profit-sharing mechanism and criticised Micron for announcing them while labour mediation was under way without first reaching an agreement with the union.

Micron, which has not linked the fiscal 2026 rewards to the labour dispute in Taiwan, did not directly address the strike threat in an emailed response to Reuters.

“We will continue listening to our team members’ perspectives and remain committed to engaging in the mediation process in good faith,” the company said.

Together, the unions represent more than 80 per cent of Micron’s roughly 15,000 employees in Taiwan, according to the Taoyuan union.

(Sept 15): Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang took a live phone call from Donald Trump during a panel discussion on Monday, allowing the US president to dismiss artificial intelligence (AI) dangers as a “hoax”.

During the call, which Huang received on stage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Trump criticised the push to slow the pace of AI development as politically motivated or a Chinese scheme. Huang agreed with the president, saying Trump had seen through the complexities of the issue.

The AI pushback is “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen”, Trump said. “And that could be political people. It could also be China.”

Even while downplaying AI risks, Huang praised an Anthropic researcher who resigned over the fears. The employee, Jacob Coxon, was courageous to voice his concerns, the CEO said. Whistle-blowers should be taken seriously inside organisations, he added.

However, the panic has created a false choice between fast innovation and AI safety, Huang said.

The potential danger of AI to humanity has become a topic of intense discussion in recent days. After Coxon resigned, saying Anthropic and OpenAI were “gambling with our lives”, calls have grown to curb the pace of development. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay — later endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — proposing a slowdown.

US tech stocks slumped on Monday over concern about a potential deceleration in spending. Shares of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, fell 3.4%.

Nvidia, whose chips help run AI models, has been the top beneficiary of a massive AI infrastructure build-out. Trump, meanwhile, has emerged as a fierce advocate for data centre construction, even in the face of growing opposition.

Trump criticised US states for refusing to give permits for the building of new data centres. Such facilities make people and states wealthy, he said.

“It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years,” he said. “It’s bigger than the internet.”

stories.title: AI power demand drives repurposing of old industries for data centres
stories.summary: Rising power demand from AI data centers is driving infrastructure companies to convert older industrial sites into data center facilities. The strategy leverages existing energy connections and assets to deploy capacity faster and help bridge a projected power shortfall for AI compute.
stories.why_it_matters: Repurposing brownfield industrial sites shortens development timelines and sidesteps the grid interconnection queues blocking greenfield projects. It also creates new value for legacy industrial landowners and shifts where data centers get built, favoring established industrial corridors over traditional tech hubs.
stories.content:
The escalating power demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centres is driving a strategic shift towards repurposing existing industrial infrastructure to meet future compute needs. London-based AI infrastructure company Teravolt highlights a significant global power shortfall, advocating for the conversion of legacy energy assets like old thermal power plants and industrial sites into data centres.Industry projections underscore the scale of this challenge. Gartner predicts world data centre power demand will surge from 104 GW in 2025 to 132 GW in 2026, reaching 290 GW by 2030. Similarly, Morgan Stanley anticipates US data centre demand could climb to 74 GW by 2028, facing a projected shortfall of approximately 49 GW.Teravolt's own analysis foresees AI demand requiring 410 GW by 2036, against an anticipated grid availability of only 170 GW, resulting in a 240 GW deficit. The company points out that while data centres can be built in one to three years, developing new grid infrastructure is a much longer process, typically spanning five to 15 years for planning, permitting, and construction.To bridge this gap, Teravolt's business model focuses on repurposing existing energy assets, such as old thermal power plants, industrial sites, or refineries. These brownfield locations often come with pre-existing infrastructure, permits, contracts, and staff, accelerating deployment. The economic viability is compelling: an aluminum smelter generating $170 to $190 of gross revenue per megawatt-hour (MWh) could be transformed into an AI data centre yielding $450 to $900 of revenue and about $300 of EBITDA per MWh.Laert Karaashev, co-founder and managing partner of Teravolt, emphasised the foundational role of power. "But the bottom layer, which is power, it is hard to imagine how to commoditize it," he stated, highlighting the years of investment required to meet energy demand. Denis Alkhazov, founder and general manager, further argued that the margin from selling AI compute is two orders of magnitude greater than from classic industries like metal production or cryptocurrency mining. "The low marginal users of power will be cannibalized by the new form of extracting value from the power," Alkhazov said.Teravolt is currently concentrating its efforts on Eastern and Southern Europe, where suitable brownfield sites are available at reasonable costs. This contrasts with the US and Western Europe, where such sites have seen significant price increases. Alkhazov noted that most customers, including mid-sized AI labs seeking 20,000 GPUs, expect delivery within 12 months or less, a timeline he described as "completely unachievable in Western markets." He added, "So you have to be creative and have to shift to other geographies to provide some solutions for that kind of demand."Given these trends, data centre operators, investors, and EPC firms should evaluate existing industrial brownfield sites for potential data centre conversion. Additionally, assessing long-term power procurement strategies is crucial, considering the projected AI-driven demand shortfalls. Monitoring global trends in repurposing legacy infrastructure for data centre development will also be key for strategic planning.

stories.title: AI Slowdown Debate Raises Questions for Asia's Chip Industry
stories.summary: Asian semiconductor and technology stocks fell after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI developers to slow the pace of capability improvements, reviving debate about whether AI infrastructure spending can be sustained. The selloff came even as AI investment continues to drive data center and power demand across the region.
stories.why_it_matters: Public warnings from leading AI labs introduce a new source of volatility for Asia's chip supply chain, which has priced in years of uninterrupted AI demand growth. If the slowdown argument gains traction, memory makers, foundries and the data center developers depending on their order books would all face re-rating.
stories.content:
- **AI chip stocks in Asia fell despite continued investment in AI infrastructure.**
- **AI spending is also driving data-centre and power demand across Asia.**

Asian semiconductor and technology stocks fell on Monday after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for companies developing advanced artificial intelligence models to slow the pace of capability improvements. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI chief Elon Musk also backed calls for a more measured pace of development amid concerns over AI safety.

The reaction was felt across several companies tied to AI infrastructure. Japan’s SoftBank fell as much as 13.2%, South Korea’s SK Hynix dropped 6.3%, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) slipped 1.2%, according to *Reuters*. Samsung Electronics closed 4.05% lower in Seoul.

US and European semiconductor stocks also declined. Nvidia fell 3%, AMD dropped 5.7%, and Dutch chip equipment maker ASML was down 5.8%, while European technology stocks fell about 2.5%.

The selloff came as investors were already scrutinising the pace of AI infrastructure spending across semiconductors, data centres, and power systems.

### AI slowdown debate meets long-term chip spending

Amodei called for a slower rate of model development in an essay published over the weekend, arguing that safety work needs more time to keep pace with increasingly capable systems. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote.

He cited advances in AI systems assisting with the development of subsequent models, as well as recent incidents involving autonomous AI agents. Amodei said these developments had increased his concerns about safeguards keeping pace with model capabilities.

OpenAI has separately slowed some development work. In August, the company said it temporarily reduced the pace of scaling after the OpenAI-Hugging Face security incident and preliminary evidence that its Astra model could meet the Critical cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework.

OpenAI said the changes included stronger isolation for research workloads, tighter network controls, and expanded monitoring. The company also said some safeguards added additional computing overhead to monitored inference workloads.

*Reuters* reported that investors were weighing whether slower development of frontier models could affect future spending on chips and data centres.

TSMC entered the second half of 2026 with a larger investment programme than previously planned. In July, the company raised its full-year capital expenditure forecast to between US$60 billion and US$64 billion, from an earlier range of US$52 billion to US$56 billion.

TSMC reported second-quarter revenue of US$40.2 billion and said AI-related demand remained strong. The company also raised its forecast for 2026 revenue growth to slightly above 40% in US dollar terms.

Those investments are planned over several years rather than around individual model launches. TSMC CEO C.C. Wei said the company works with customers and their customers on multi-year product roadmaps and production plans, with the process of developing technology, preparing capacity, and reaching high-volume production taking more than five years.

TSMC is also building 13 leading-edge semiconductor and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan as part of its broader capacity expansion.

Memory suppliers have also increased production plans around AI servers. Samsung began commercial shipments of HBM4 earlier this year and said it expects its HBM sales to more than triple in 2026 compared with 2025.

Samsung said in its second-quarter results that its memory business recorded another quarterly high while focusing production on server products. The company expects demand for server DRAM, enterprise SSDs, and HBM to remain supported by AI infrastructure capital expenditure during the second half of 2026.

SK Hynix has also tied its capacity plans to multi-year customer agreements. The company said in July that it had completed long-term supply agreements with around 10 customers, including strategic customers, and was discussing further multi-year contracts with other large clients.

The company approved another 54 trillion won in semiconductor investment in August. The plan includes 35.2 trillion won for a new DRAM fab in Yongin and 19.1 trillion won for a NAND fab in Cheongju, with cleanroom openings scheduled for 2029 and 2028 respectively. SK Hynix said capacity additions would be aligned with customer demand.

The company said its longer-term manufacturing and packaging investments would be phased according to customer demand and investment efficiency.

Long investment cycles are also evident in chipmaking equipment. ASML’s current extreme ultraviolet lithography systems, which are used to manufacture advanced chips, are largely sold out through 2027, according to *Reuters*.

Samsung and SK Hynix plan to introduce ASML’s newer High Numerical Aperture EUV systems into memory production from 2028, while TSMC plans to use the technology for advanced-node high-volume manufacturing from 2030.

The High-NA systems cost about US$400 million each, roughly twice the price of ASML’s existing EUV machines.

Frontier-model training is only one source of AI computing demand. Deployed AI systems also require infrastructure for inference, including agentic workloads.

TSMC said in July that the expansion of agentic AI was increasing demand for CPUs inside AI data centres alongside AI accelerators. Wei said the company was working with CPU customers using x86, Arm, and RISC-V architectures to prepare technology and capacity for those workloads.

Samsung has also linked memory demand to AI inference. The company said earlier this year that it was expanding sales of high-performance NAND products used for inference workloads, alongside HBM, server DRAM, and enterprise SSD products.

SK Hynix’s next-generation HBM4E memory is also being developed for both AI training and inference. The company said the product improves data processing performance and power efficiency for AI data centres and large-scale computing systems.

Spending forecasts also remain high. Morgan Stanley Research estimates that capital expenditure by the five largest US technology companies will increase from nearly US$800 billion in 2026 to around US$1.2 trillion in 2027 and US$1.4 trillion in 2028.

The spending includes chips, servers, data centres, power infrastructure, and other capacity required for AI services. UBS said in July that near-term AI spending remained strong, while flagging pressure on hyperscaler free cash flow and the risk of slower spending growth after 2027.

### AI infrastructure spending is reaching data centres and power grids

On September 8, OpenAI and Australian infrastructure company Firmus announced a multi-year agreement covering dedicated AI compute capacity at two Firmus data-centre sites in Malaysia.

Firmus said OpenAI would become an anchor customer and that its contracted capacity across all customers had risen above 900 MW. The company has seven planned or operating AI data-centre sites across Australia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia.

Malaysia’s Energy Commission has already identified data-centre expansion as one factor behind higher electricity demand. It said electricity demand reached new peaks in 2025, driven by factors including economic activity, electrification, industrial expansion, weather conditions, and data-centre growth.

*Reuters* reported that data centres accounted for 9.3% of electricity consumption in Peninsular Malaysia during part of August, compared with an average of about 7% in 2026. Officials estimate the share could rise to as much as 31% by 2035.

Tenaga Nasional had signed electricity supply agreements with 49 data centres by September 2025, representing maximum demand of 7.1 GW, according to data published by the Malaysian Investment Development Authority. Actual utilisation reached 710 MW at the time, up 75% from the end of 2024.

South Korea is also planning for higher electricity demand from semiconductor production and AI data centres. Energy Minister Kim Sung-whan said in September that these projects could add between 25 GW and 30 GW to national electricity demand.

The projected increase is being incorporated into the government’s long-term electricity planning. Nuclear power currently accounts for nearly a third of South Korea’s electricity generation.

Grid financing has also become part of the semiconductor expansion plans. *Reuters* reported on Monday that Korea Electric Power Corp had proposed requiring Samsung and SK Hynix to provide around 25 trillion won in advance payments for electricity infrastructure serving planned semiconductor clusters. Both companies rejected the proposal.

Samsung and SK Hynix declined to comment on the proposal. A company official told *Reuters* that the chipmakers questioned whether such large upfront payments were necessary, citing uncertainty over the long-term durability of semiconductor demand.

The proposed infrastructure would supply planned semiconductor mega-clusters. South Korea’s government has separately accelerated semiconductor projects originally expected around 2045, with completion now targeted for the early 2030s.

stories.content:
The global artificial intelligence (AI) sector is facing significant challenges in building infrastructure fast enough to meet escalating demand, according to a Goldman Sachs report. This infrastructure bottleneck is occurring even as AI's largest economic opportunities, particularly in the physical world and broader economy, remain largely untapped.Goldman Sachs projects that global hyperscaler capital expenditure (CapEx) will exceed $760 billion in 2026, equating to approximately $2 billion per day. This substantial investment is spread across various geographies, with US hyperscalers accounting for the largest share, complemented by structural capital deployment from Middle East sovereign wealth funds, European industrial investment, and Asian regional supply chains.The scale of demand is further evidenced by Google's agreement to pay SpaceX around $920 million monthly, totalling nearly $30 billion through mid-2029, for access to approximately 110,000 Nvidia GPUs. Simultaneously, grid operators are contending with interconnection requests that carry energy requirements far exceeding their planning models from three years ago, leading to multiyear backlogs for electrical distribution equipment from major manufacturers.

Against this backdrop, fully islanded data centers are gaining traction as an alternative for hyperscale AI infrastructure, particularly due to increasing grid connection delays. Goldman Sachs notes that a year ago, such solutions were rare, but in the last 12 to 18 months, they have moved from an edge case to a credible development pathway, driven by both interconnection delays and the economics of AI compute. Estimates now suggest that one-third of future capacity could be islanded.

stories.title: Building trusted access into Australia's next generation of data centres
stories.summary: Open, interoperable access systems may spare Australian data centres costly upgrades as AI-driven demand and security needs evolve over decades.
stories.content:
Tue, 15th Sep 2026 (Yesterday)
Australia's data centre market is entering a new phase. The rapid adoption of cloud computing and AI is driving unprecedented demand for digital infrastructure, with developers planning facilities at a scale that would have seemed extraordinary only a few years ago.

This reflects more than the growth of an individual industry. Data centres are rapidly becoming critical national infrastructure - the physical foundation for Australia's businesses, government services, communications and increasingly its AI capabilities.

Much of the conversation around new facilities understandably focuses on power, cooling, connectivity, resilience and sustainability. Yet there is another foundational question that deserves equal attention: how will people move securely through the facility, today and for decades to come?

For developers and operators, physical access control is no longer simply about securing doors. It is about establishing trusted identity throughout the facility and ensuring the right people can access the right areas at the right time.

Data centres are designed to operate for decades, so while the facility itself may remain in service for many years, security requirements, authentication technologies and operational needs will continue to evolve. The access-control infrastructure must be able to support that evolution.

### Layered security is the starting point

Layered security has long been fundamental to data centre design. Access privileges become increasingly restrictive as people move from the perimeter through building entrances and into data halls and other sensitive areas. Authentication requirements can strengthen at each layer according to the individual's role, the sensitivity of the environment and the level of risk. But layered access itself is no longer a differentiator. Any credible security architecture should be capable of implementing it.

The more important question is what sits underneath that layered model. Effective physical security starts with confidence in identity. Employees, contractors, service providers and visitors all need to be authenticated securely and consistently, while operators need the flexibility to apply different levels of access according to role and circumstance. This becomes particularly important as digital and physical security increasingly converge.

### The long-term risk is building yourself into a corner

A data centre's access-control system may appear to be a relatively small decision during the design and construction phase. Its consequences, however, can last for decades.

A closed, single-vendor architecture may perform perfectly well on day one, but over time it can constrain the operator's choices. New authentication technologies may require wholesale replacement. Expansion may mean purchasing more proprietary hardware and integrating with other systems can become unnecessarily complex. The system that initially looked like a safe choice can ultimately become the barrier preventing the facility from adapting as security requirements change over time.

For infrastructure intended to support Australia's long-term digital and data sovereignty ambitions, that is a significant but avoidable risk. This is why open architecture matters.

Open, interoperable platforms allow operators to integrate access control with a wider ecosystem of technologies, including video surveillance, identity management and operational systems. They also make it easier to introduce new authentication technologies as requirements evolve.

The principle is straightforward: operators should be able to select the technologies that best meet their requirements today while retaining the flexibility to adopt new solutions as those requirements change.

### Building for Australia's next data centre decade

The scale of Australia's data centre growth makes these decisions increasingly consequential. Physical access control may not be the most visible element of a data centre build. But it is one of the foundations that will remain in place long after construction is complete.

The question for operators is therefore bigger than which reader or credential to specify.

They should ask whether the access-control architecture is built around trusted identity, whether it supports open standards and interoperability, whether it can accommodate future authentication technologies, and whether the provider and partner ecosystem will be there to support the facility throughout its operational life.

Get that foundation right, and Australia's data centres will have the freedom to adapt as the technology around them changes. Get it wrong, and every future decision becomes harder.

stories.title: AirTrunk, Emergence Quantum Partner to Advance Next-Gen Cryogenic Data Centre
stories.summary: AirTrunk has signed a partnership and memorandum of understanding with deep tech firm Emergence Quantum to develop cryogenic cooling and quantum computing capabilities for next-generation data centers. Cryogenic cooling can significantly boost the speed and energy efficiency of conventional silicon chips, and the same technology underpins quantum computing systems.
stories.why_it_matters: The tie-up positions AirTrunk to host quantum and cryo-cooled workloads before they become mainstream, potentially defining a new facility category beyond today's air- and liquid-cooled designs. For the broader industry, it suggests cooling innovation is becoming a competitive differentiator rather than just an engineering concern.
stories.content:
Hyperscale datacentre specialist AirTrunk announced today a partnership and MOU with deep tech company Emergence Quantum (EQ) to bring cryogenic cooling and quantum computing to next-generation data centres.

Cryo-cooling can significantly improve the speed and energy-efficiency of today’s silicon computer chips, enabling faster computation with less power. The same cryotechnology is also foundational to many futuristic computing systems including quantum.

Beyond the increased performance of hardware, the two companies will work closely together on cryogenic technologies that can also reduce the cooling water needs of data centres while simultaneously enabling giga-Watt power storage for leveraging intermittent supplies of renewable energy. Cryo-cooling offers further promise in the context of carbon capture.

The partnership reflects two of AirTrunk’s core commitments to the communities where it operates: safely delivering the critical infrastructure that underpins everyday life, and being a responsible user of energy and water. By exploring technologies that could deliver more computing capability while using resources more efficiently, AirTrunk is looking at how the next generation of digital infrastructure can support growing digital demand responsibly.

AirTrunk Vice President for Innovation and Intelligence, Jose Castaneda, says the partnership is part of a commitment to continuously explore new approaches and technologies that drive the future of data centres and foster Australia’s technological leadership.

“We are continuously redefining data centres with cutting-edge technologies that improve performance, efficiency and sustainability. As digital demand grows, our responsibility is not only to provide the secure and resilient infrastructure our customers and communities rely on, but to find new ways to deliver that infrastructure more efficiently. This partnership with EQ challenges the status quo and is a great example of how data centres can act as broader enablers of innovation in our communities.”

Emergence Quantum Co-founder and CEO Professor David Reilly says, “It’s been understood for decades that computers run significantly faster and more efficiently in the cold, but there are challenges and costs to cooling that have so-far limited this approach to niche applications. The scale of data centres and tiny size of transistors today changes all that — the cryo-computing epoch has arrived.”

Dr Arman Siahvashi, Emergence Quantum Head of Cryogenics noted, “In addition to our abundant renewable energy opportunities, Australia also has existing deep expertise in industrial scale cryogenics that underpin natural gas mining and hydrogen fuel cell technology. To think that this cryo-infrastructure and know-how could now be deployed to enable next-generation data centres is a tantalising opportunity for Australia.”

The partnership brings together deep expertise in cryogenic computing, thermal engineering, and quantum technologies, data centre architecture, and real-world techno-economic models that can prove out the performance opportunities for cryo-data centres. The collaboration is part of AirTrunk’s broader goal to build data centre infrastructure that is quantum ready and able to embed cryogenic cooling into overall data centre campus setup.

Professor Thomas Ohki, Co-founder and CTO of Emergence Quantum, has been working on various cryogenic computing platforms for decades: “For us, cryogenic data centres are an inevitable reality — this cooling technology is needed for high-speed efficient silicon chips, superconducting logic, and ultimately quantum computing. All flavours of qubits need cryogenics one way or another.”

The collaboration puts AirTrunk’s community commitments into practice: exploring new ways to safely deliver the critical digital infrastructure people and businesses increasingly rely on, while being a responsible user of energy and water. Cryogenic technologies have the potential to improve computing efficiency, reduce cooling water requirements and support large-scale energy storage, helping future data centres meet growing digital demand while making more efficient use of shared resources.

AirTrunk Innovation Strategy Manager Harshit Sharma noted “We recognise that quantum computing in a data centre is much more than plugging-in a physics experiment in the data hall. At scale, these systems will require extensive cryo-cooling infrastructure. This partnership is looking to deploy that cryo-infrastructure in a way that improves the performance of today’s silicon chips, all-the-while paving the road to quantum.”

Beyond the technology itself, the partnership has the potential to strengthen capability in next-generation digital infrastructure by bringing together local expertise in cryogenics, quantum technologies and hyperscale data centres. It reflects AirTrunk’s broader ambition to create shared value through the infrastructure it delivers — supporting innovation, capability and opportunities that can contribute to more resilient economies and communities.

University of Sydney Vice-Chancellor and President Professor Mark Scott said the partnership demonstrated the strength of local expertise in cryogenics, quantum technologies and hyperscale data centres.

“This ambitious partnership between AirTrunk and Emergence Quantum promises to bring about a new phase in data centre technology, one that is focused on hitting environmental milestones,” he said.

“Here we have two organisations with a strong connection to the University of Sydney turning research into commercially significant technology.”

## Key points

- Digital Canberra is exploring future options for its private cloud platform, currently run on VMware software and Dell hardware, as warranty expiry looms.

The relatively new ACT government directorate is home to “digital technology, data and security systems across ACT government” as well as “Canberra’s strategy for a connected digital future”.

One of its capabilities is the ACT compute hosting platform, effectively a private cloud, that will require a “refresh”.

Digital Canberra recently revealed that “the majority of the ACT compute platform reaches warranty expiry between March and September 2027, with only a subset of newer Dell MX760c blade server infrastructure remaining supported until July 2029.”

“Continuing operation beyond the current hardware lifecycle will increase the risk of hardware failure, reduced vendor supportability, increased operating costs and place constraints on future virtualisation platform upgrades from the current VMWare Cloud Foundations (VCF) platform,” it said.

A Digital Canberra spokesperson was unable to provide any additional detail on which architectural components of the platform come up for renewal or refresh next year, citing a current request for information process that is now underway.

However, the need for future options is driven both by warranty pressures and the criticality of the platform to ACT government digital services delivery.

“The VCF platform is a critical ACT government shared service supporting approximately 1400 virtual machines across four environments [three data centres and a virtual infrastructure testing capability],” it said.

“These underpin a significant number of business and citizen-facing digital services.

“The ACT government is seeking to establish the most appropriate method to maintain the capability provided from these environments.”

Digital Canberra said that the refresh program already had a “defined budget”.

“We are engaging with industry to understand what industry can realistically deliver against the budget based on current market costs,” it said.

“The ACT government is seeking options to deliver the most pragmatic and cost-effective solution to ensure this platform remains operable and supportable into the future.”

Digital Canberra’s budget statement for 2026-27 notes that one of the directorate’s priorities this financial year is to “consolidate the ACT Government’s technology footprint by prioritising fewer, scalable whole-of-government platforms that deliver full function capabilities while maintaining

the agility to adapt and implement change efficiently.”

stories.title: Global AI stocks fall as industry chiefs call for slowing development
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-linked stocks plunged across the globe on Monday after leaders of the biggest AI companies warned of risks from rapid development, the starkest threat yet to the billions of dollars being poured into the industry that have pushed world markets to record highs.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
BENGALURU/SINGAPORE (Sept 14): Artificial intelligence (AI)-linked stocks plunged across the globe on Monday after leaders of the biggest AI companies warned of risks from rapid development, the starkest threat yet to the billions of dollars being poured into the industry that have pushed world markets to record highs.

The sell-off rippled through the industry, where companies are increasingly relying on debt and circular financing to fund ambitious AI spending plans even as global borrowing costs, reflected in multi-year-high bond yields, continue to rise.

Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei, in a lengthy essay shared on X on Saturday, called on AI companies to slow the rate at which they advance model capabilities amid mounting fears of misuse of AI. Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei.

Altman also said the company would not proceed with an IPO this year, citing safety concerns.

Wall Street's elite tech index, the Nasdaq 100, slid 1.7% in early trading as chip stocks, which have led the AI sugar rush, fell the most.

"If this does lead to sort of a slowdown and a rethink of AI spending, that will have ramifications for the economy and some important sectors of the stock market, because essentially, we've been running hot based on AI spending," said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers.

The Philadelphia chip index dropped 6%, with Nvidia down 3.5%, Advanced Micro Devices off 5.6% and Micron falling 6.7%, while Musk's SpaceX dropped 2.5%.

Semiconductor equipment makers Lam Research and Applied Materials tumbled 8% and 7%, respectively, while tech utilities Bloom Energy lost 8.9% and GE Vernova declined 7.6%.

Europe's tech sector fell 2.3%, dragged down by ASML's 6.7% decline, alongside steep losses in Infineon and Siemens Energy, while in Asia, SoftBank plunged as much as 13.2% and chipmakers TSMC and SK Hynix also retreated.

Alarm about the potential harm from AI spiked earlier this month when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, stating that the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

A few days later, the San Francisco-based AI lab released a threat intelligence report detailing how its Claude AI models were used for activities ranging from weapons development and cyber operations to surveillance and fraud.

Over the weekend, Amodei wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable of taking over the entire internet potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage". Separately, OpenAI's Altman said in an interview that risks of human extinction posed by AI were "unacceptable".

And while several US lawmakers have raised concern about AI's rapid progress and called for new rules, US President Donald Trump on Sunday likened AI critics to "very negative forces" bringing up scenarios that will not happen, and said he wanted to make sure that the US remains the industry leader.

AI-related trades have powered much of the gains in global equities since OpenAI released ChatGPT in 2022, but more recently cyberattacks by rogue AI agents and public discontent with data centre construction have raised opposition to the development of the industry.

The US and Chinese governments are expected to hold AI safety talks as part of bilateral discussions taking place this month, *Reuters* reported. But China's state-backed *Global Times* blasted the Anthropic essay in an editorial, calling it a "Cold War playbook" intended to curb the country's technological development.

Some investors dismissed the warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Michael Burry, whose prescient bets against the US housing market before the 2008 financial crisis were chronicled in the movie "The Big Short", said in a message on X the warnings were "hype and puffery" and "cover for real uncontrollable slowing growth".

Others argued that record capital spending commitments suggest AI development is unlikely to slow, such as Morgan Stanley's Brian Nowak who forecast earlier this year that AI spending will surpass US$1.2 trillion (RM4.85 trillion) by 2027.

"The key question is whether this is the first sign that the extraordinary AI investment cycle might eventually moderate. For now, that seems unlikely. The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it's difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead," Deutsche Bank said in a note.

Meanwhile, Amodei's Anthropic has pushed ahead with its public debut, expected next month as sources told *Reuters* that the company is in talks to bring in Nvidia as an anchor investor.

Japanese chipmaker Kioxia Holdings is also considering raising at least US$10 billion by listing American depositary receipts, a report said.
